n:
The people and leaders of the northern kingdom hadn’t loved God. They hadn’t shown faithfulness to him. The way that God explained this was like bringing charges against them in court. God accused them of not being faithful to the Mount Sinai covenant.

The people and leaders of the northern kingdom didn’t honour God as God. They stole and told lies. They committed murder and adultery. These things went against the Ten Commandments. The ways that God’s people acted brought harm to the land and animals around them. This showed that they weren’t being rulers of God’s creation like they should be.

They burnt incense to false gods on high places. They killed human beings and sacrificed them to false gods. This showed that God’s people didn’t recognise who God is. They didn’t recognise how he wanted to be worshipped.

The priests didn’t lead the people in following the Law of Moses. Many prophets didn’t speak the truth to the people. God’s people made fun of prophets who did speak the truth. The kings and princes didn’t follow God’s rules for kings recorded in Deuteronomy 17:14–20. They depended on the strength of their large armies and the armies of other nations. They trusted nations like Egypt and Assyria to save them when they were attacked. They didn’t cry out to God when they needed help.

Because of all of these things, God had made a decision. He would no longer keep the covenant curses from coming upon them. He would allow the northern kingdom to be destroyed by the armies of Assyria. The people and leaders of the northern kingdom would suffer terribly. Many would be killed and many would be forced to leave their land. They would be forced to live in Assyria and other nations. This was the exile of the northern kingdom.

God was very sad about this decision. He didn’t want it to happen. He wanted to bless and heal his people and give them success. But he could only do that if they changed their ways and did what was right and fair. He could do it if they recognised that he is God. He could do it if they asked him to forgive them. That was why God sent them messages through Hosea. God understood that his people refused to turn back to him. They refused to repent of their sin with their whole heart. But God’s heart was full of kindness, pity and mercy towards them. He described himself as Israel’s father. God was gentle and tender towards his son. He didn’t want his son to be destroyed.

God promised something for after the time of judgement. He promised to bring his people back from exile. Then they would follow God faithfully and he would love them freely.

This collection of Hosea’s prophecies is mostly in the order in which he made them. The prophecies began early in his ministry when Jeroboam II's was king. They ended just before Israel's destruction in 722 BC.

Hosea shares God's accusations against Israel, warns them of severe consequences for their sins, and ends with a promise of future restoration.
*My son*: The Lord adopted Israel when he delivered them from Egypt. This verse refers to Jesus in {{Matthew 2:15|Matthew 2:15}} (see study note on Matthew 4:1–11).

God grieved over Israel’s unfaithfulness. Even after all he had done for them, Israel had turned into a rebellious people. Justice required serious punishment, but the final decision about Israel’s future would come from God’s tender compassion for his people, not from an abstract rule.
Despite God's love, Israel acted like a rebellious child, offering sacrifices to Baal. The punishment for a rebellious son was death ({{Deuteronomy 21:18-21|Deuteronomy 21:18–21}}).
God cared for the young nation of Israel with kindness and love.
Since the Israelites refused to return to the Lord, they would go back to Egypt and serve Assyria. Their past slavery in Egypt symbolized their future exile in Assyria.

- Although justice required Israel's death, the Lord hesitated to give up Israel, let them go, or destroy his son. 

- Admah and Zeboiim were cities near Sodom and Gomorrah that God completely destroyed ({{Deuteronomy 29:23|Deuteronomy 29:23}}). 

- In Hebrew thought, the heart is the center of intellect and will.

- *I will not*: The Lord alone would decide Israel’s fate. God repeated *I will not* three times to stress his choice not to destroy his people completely. 

- The reason for this divine decision is, *I am … the Holy One among you*. God's holiness sets him apart from all creation (see “God’s Absolute Holiness” Theme Note). An offended person might destroy a rebel out of anger and spite. The *Holy One* does not act from those motives.
Israel’s sin would not be the final word. God, in his holy love, would roar like a lion (see {{Amos 1:2|Amos 1:2}}; {{Amos 3:8|3:8}}) to call his people home from exile in Babylon.
Israel has engaged in deception and dishonesty since Jacob's time.

- *a covenant with Assyria*: To save his land, Hoshea became a vassal of King Shalmaneser of Assyria ({{2 Kings 17:3|2 Kings 17:3}}). Hoshea soon rebelled against Shalmaneser by withholding tribute and sought support from King So of Egypt ({{2 Kings 17:4|2 Kings 17:4}}). 

- *east wind*: See study note on Job 38:24–27.

- *he grasped his brother’s heel* (literally *he supplanted his brother*): The Hebrew verb *‘aqab* is the root of Jacob's name. Even before birth, Jacob lived up to his name by supplanting his brother Esau ({{Genesis 25:26|Genesis 25:26}}).

- As an adult, Jacob even fought with God (see {{Genesis 32:22-30|Genesis 32:22–30}}) and was renamed “Israel,” meaning “God fights.”
The Lord urged Israel to stop living like Jacob. Instead, they should return to God and act with love and justice.

- During the reign of Jeroboam II (793–753 BC), Israelite merchants became very wealthy. They often used deceitful business practices like dishonest scales (see {{Amos 8:5-6|Amos 8:5–6}}). 

- The Hebrew term for merchants is *kena‘an* (“Canaan”). Canaanite traders were known in the ancient world for their crafty dealings. The Israelites imitated their pagan neighbors in both religion and commerce.

*I will again make you dwell in tents*: This judgment on the wealthy Israelite merchants means they will return to the simple homes of the exodus. There is also hope here. God's plan to save Israel will start again in the wilderness (see {{Hosea 2:14-15|Hosea 2:14–15}}).
Gilead and Gilgal were cities where Israelites worshiped Baal instead of the Lord (see {{Hosea 4:15|Hosea 4:15}}; {{Hosea 6:8|6:8}}; {{Hosea 9:15|9:15}}).
*by a prophet*: Moses obeyed God faithfully, which contrasts with Israel's disobedience.

- At the height of its power, the tribe of Ephraim caused fear among other Israelites (see {{Isaiah 7:2|Isaiah 7:2}}). 

- *he *[Ephraim] *died*: Because of their idolatry, they separated themselves from the Lord, the only true source of life.

- The Hebrew word for idols is the same as the one used for the golden calf ({{Exodus 32:4|Exodus 32:4}}, {{Exodus 32:8|8}}; see also {{Hosea 10:5-6|Hosea 10:5–6}}; {{Amos 5:5-6|Amos 5:5–6}}). 

- *Kiss the calves!*: Canaanite religious ceremonies involved kissing images of Baal ({{1 Kings 19:18|1 Kings 19:18}}).

- God judged idolatrous Ephraim by saying they would disappear (compare {{Hosea 6:4|Hosea 6:4}}). 

- Mist, dew, chaff, and smoke all represent things that do not last.
*there is no Savior*: The Lord proved this to Israel during the exodus and their time in the wilderness.
*their hearts became proud, and. … forgot Me*: They did not rely on the Lord for safety. Instead, they trusted their kings, armies, and wealth (see {{Hosea 2:13|Hosea 2:13}}).
God judged Israel using the Assyrian army as his tool for punishment. The description of God's attack highlights the Assyrians' cruelty to those they conquered.
*Me … your helper*: See {{Psalm 70:5|Psalms 70:5}}; {{Psalm 115:9|115:9}}; {{Psalm 121:2|121:2}}; {{Psalm 124:8|124:8}}. Israel's sin had turned their helper into their destroyer.

*Where is your king*: When Hoshea's alliance with Egypt failed (see {{Hosea 12:1|Hosea 12:1}}), he attempted to make peace with Assyria. However, they captured and imprisoned him ({{2 Kings 17:4|2 Kings 17:4}}). The Israelites had depended on their armies and kings for salvation instead of the Lord, and now no one could save them.
Israel had chosen its kings without asking the Lord, so now he would take them away in anger.
God had carefully stored up the record of Israel’s sin and guilt. He could not escape his punishment.
Israel was like a child in the womb who resisted being born (*an unwise son*). Amazingly, Israel preferred to stay in the womb rather than receive life from the Lord.

*Sheol* refers to the realm of the dead (see {{Job 3:11-19|Job 3:11–19}}; see also study note on Job 7:9). The Lord rules over Sheol and could save Israel if he chose to. However, he will not show mercy to the Israelites and calls upon death to punish them.

- In 722 BC, Assyria captured Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom ({{2 Kings 17:5-6|2 Kings 17:5–6}}). Thousands died during the three-year siege, and many more were exiled. This happened because they rebelled against their God. 

- The terrible act of killing pregnant women is also mentioned in {{Amos 1:13|Amos 1:13}} and {{2 Kings 15:16|2 Kings 15:16}}.
Destruction was not God's final message to his covenant people. Although judgment must happen, God's healing and restoring grace is stronger than human sin.

- Hosea created a prayer of confession to guide his people back to the Lord. God’s prophets felt both God's anger over Israel’s rebellion and the people's suffering (see also {{Daniel 9:4-19|Daniel 9:4–19}}). 

- *Take away all our iniquity*: The Israelites should rely on God’s mercy and grace, openly admitting their many sins. 

- *that we may present the fruit of our lips*: Israel often offered animal sacrifices for sin, but the Lord made it clear that sacrifices were not the answer (see {{Hosea 6:6|Hosea 6:6}}). Israel should give God true repentance.

The Israelites must give up their reliance on idols, foreign alliances, and their military strength. Even though they were God's children ({{Hosea 11:1|Hosea 11:1}}), their rebellion made them orphans. When they sincerely and fully repented, they could find mercy again.
*I will heal their apostasy*: Only God can cure the disease of sin. The Lord heals all our physical and spiritual diseases ({{Psalm 103:3|Psalm 103:3}}).

- *like the dew*: In Israel's semi-desert climate, dew provided essential moisture for life ({{Genesis 27:28|Genesis 27:28}}; {{Deuteronomy 33:28|Deuteronomy 33:28}}). 

- *take root*: When Israel remained faithful to their covenant with the Lord, they became solid and stable like the majestic cedars in Lebanon ({{Psalm 92:12|Psalm 92:12}}).
Hosea describes the effect of God’s healing love on repentant Israel. God promises to provide the fertility that Israel had sought from the baals.
*in his shade*: A safe and comforting place ({{Psalm 91:1|Psalm 91:1}}; {{Isaiah 25:4|Isaiah 25:4}}).
Hosea urges Israel one last time to avoid idols. Their life comes only from the Lord, who is like an evergreen tree that always produces fruit.
This final verse praises Hosea's words to wise and thoughtful believers of all generations.
